notes.b: Voluntary organisations are non-profit bodies run largely by volunteers. Many receive some State funding, but they are independent of government.
points: The Society of St Vincent de Paul works through local volunteer conferences that visit households in their area confidentially and assess the help needed.
St Vincent de Paul provides food or fuel vouchers, help with essential household bills, school books and uniforms, furniture and emergency accommodation.
St Vincent de Paul raises its funds through charity shops and public and church collections.
Simon Community provides support and emergency accommodation to people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness.
Focus Ireland works to prevent homelessness and provides accommodation, training in personal and life skills, and information on job opportunities.
Voluntary organisations direct clients to State entitlements, MABS and Citizens Information, linking people to services they are entitled to.
Voluntary organisations act as pressure groups: they gather evidence on local need and campaign for changes in public policy.
Unfunded services, such as volunteer-run listening services, fill gaps that statutory services do not cover.

notes.b: Community initiatives are locally run responses to unemployment and early school leaving, often funded by the State.
points: Community education centres offer adult literacy and numeracy classes and personal development courses, often for people who left school early.
Community training workshops offer practical and vocational skills, often with a route to a recognised qualification.
Education and Training Boards provide adult and further education, and many community courses are delivered through them.
Community Employment provides temporary paid work on local projects such as the environment, heritage, sport and tourism, for long-term unemployed people.
Community-based projects build confidence, work experience and social networks, which help people move back into paid work.
Local groups identify training needs in their area, such as skills gaps in the local economy, and design courses to meet them.

notes.b: A co-operative is a business owned and democratically controlled by its members, who share its surplus.
points: Each member has one vote regardless of how much they have invested, and members elect the board.
The surplus is shared among members in proportion to their use of the co-operative or reinvested in the business, rather than paid to outside shareholders.
Worker co-operatives are owned by their employees, consumer co-operatives by their customers, and housing co-operatives by their tenants.
Credit unions are member-owned co-operatives that offer savings accounts and affordable loans, a key service for low-income households.
A community co-operative can run a shop, a childcare service or local transport where no private business will, creating local jobs.
Profits stay with members and the local area rather than leaving the community with outside owners.

notes.b: A cottage industry is small-scale production carried out in the home or a small workshop, using traditional or handmade skills.
points: Products include hand-knitted Aran jumpers, weaving, pottery and other handmade crafts, often sold to local and tourist markets.
Cottage industries give families an extra or sole source of income, especially in rural areas where other employment is limited.
They need little capital, because the equipment is simple and production takes place at home.
Limitations include seasonal or irregular income, small output, limited marketing reach and reliance on tourism.
Local Enterprise Offices can help producers with training and grants to develop craft businesses.
The Combat Poverty Agency was a State body that researched poverty, advised government and funded anti-poverty projects.
It no longer exists as an independent agency, so current answers should name the bodies and organisations that carry out this work today.

keyTerms.definition: A non-profit body, run largely by volunteers, that provides services or campaigns on a social issue independently of government.
A business owned and democratically controlled by its members, who share its surplus.
A member-owned co-operative that offers savings accounts and affordable loans to its members.
Small-scale production of goods, often in the home, using traditional or handmade skills.
Locally delivered courses, such as adult literacy, that help people who left school early return to learning.
Temporary paid work on local community projects, offered to long-term unemployed people to build work experience.
An organisation that campaigns to influence public opinion and government policy on a particular issue.

questions.prompt: Describe how a credit union or a community co-operative can help people on low incomes.
questions.model: A credit union is a member-owned co-operative that offers savings accounts and affordable loans, giving low-income households access to credit without relying on high-cost lenders. Members have one vote each, so decisions are made democratically. A community co-operative can run a shop, childcare service or local transport where no private business will, which keeps essential services and jobs in the area. Profits or surpluses stay with members and the local community rather than going to outside owners.

questions.prompt: Discuss the contribution of voluntary organisations and community-based education, training and employment initiatives to responding to poverty in Ireland. Refer to named organisations or initiatives.
questions.model: Voluntary organisations: non-profit bodies run largely by volunteers, independent of government, though many receive State funding. The Society of St Vincent de Paul uses local volunteer conferences to visit households confidentially, providing food or fuel vouchers, help with bills, school books and uniforms, and emergency accommodation; it raises funds through charity shops and collections. Simon Community and Focus Ireland respond to homelessness, providing emergency accommodation, training and information on job opportunities. Voluntary organisations link clients to State entitlements and to MABS and Citizens Information, act as pressure groups by campaigning for policy change, and fill gaps through unfunded services. Community-based education, training and employment: community education centres provide adult literacy and numeracy classes for people who left school early; training workshops offer vocational skills with recognised qualifications; Education and Training Boards deliver adult and further education; Community Employment gives long-term unemployed people temporary paid work on local projects, building work experience. These initiatives respond to local needs and build confidence and networks that help people return to paid work. Co-operatives and cottage industries: co-operatives keep services and jobs in a community, and cottage industries give families an extra or sole income with little capital. Assessment: voluntary and community responses are quick, personal and local, reaching people statutory services miss, but they depend on volunteers and funding and do not remove the structural causes of poverty, so they complement State responsibility rather than replace it.
